title: The memory collar
summary: The **collar** (also called wrapper or interface) is the small piece of logic that sits around every memory. It decides who talks to the memory — the functional logic or MBIST — and often checks the read data. It must do this without slowing the chip down.
objectives: Draw the functional and test paths through a collar.
Explain where the comparator can sit and why.
Explain the bypass that lets scan test the logic around a memory.
Describe how pipelining keeps the test at full speed.

steps.title: Functional path
steps.md: In normal operation the functional logic drives the memory's address, data and write-enable through an **input mux**; the read data goes out to the functional logic.

steps.title: Test path
steps.md: When **test_mode** is 1, the input mux takes address, data and commands from the **MBIST controller** instead.

steps.title: Comparator
steps.md: The read data is compared with the **expected data** from the controller. A mismatch is a **fail**.

steps.title: Bypass
steps.md: For **scan test** of the logic around the memory, an output mux can route the memory's inputs directly to its outputs, so the memory looks like a wire and the surrounding logic stays testable.

blocks.title: The mux is on the functional path
blocks.md: Every functional access passes through the collar's input mux, so it adds a little **delay** to timing-critical paths. Collars are designed to be as thin as possible, and memory compilers often offer memories with a built-in test port to avoid the extra mux.

blocks.caption: Local compare sends one fail bit back; central compare sends every read bit back

items.title: Comparator in the collar (local compare)
items.md: The controller sends the **expected data** to the collar; the collar compares and sends back only a **fail bit**. Few wires go back to the controller — important when one controller serves many wide memories. This is the most common choice.

items.title: Comparator in the controller (central compare)
items.md: The collar sends the **full read data** back to the controller. Simple collars, but many long wires (a 128-bit memory sends 128 bits), which costs area and makes at-speed timing harder.

items.title: Per-bit fail information
items.md: For diagnosis and repair it is useful to know **which bit** failed, not just *that* a fail happened. Local comparators can keep a per-bit (or per-column) fail flag.

blocks.md:
Scan and ATPG test the **logic** of the chip. A memory is a black box for them: data written into it cannot be predicted by the ATPG tool, and the logic between the memory and the next flip-flops — the **shadow logic** — becomes hard to test.

The collar helps in one of two ways:

- **Bypass**: in scan mode the memory's inputs are routed straight to its outputs, so ATPG sees a simple path.
- **Observation flip-flops**: the memory's inputs are captured in extra scan flip-flops, and its outputs are driven by others.

items.text: The CPU writes data into the cache memory
The controller writes background D into every address
The memory is bypassed so ATPG can test the logic behind it
Read data is compared with expected data

blocks.md: MBIST must run at the memory's **full clock frequency** to catch dynamic and recovery faults. But the controller may sit far from the memory, and wires across a big chip are slow. The solution is **pipelining**: registers in the collar hold address, data and commands for one clock, and the comparison happens one or two clocks after the read.

steps.title: Clock 1
steps.md: The controller sends *read address 5*. Nothing has reached the memory yet.

steps.title: Clock 2
steps.md: Address 5 is read by the memory while the controller already sends *read address 6*.

steps.title: Clock 3
steps.md: The collar compares the data of address 5 — two clocks after it was sent — while address 6 is read and address 7 sent.

steps.title: Clock 4
steps.md: And so on: one operation per clock, every stage busy.

blocks.title: The memory still sees back-to-back operations
blocks.md: Pipelining delays the **commands and the compare**, not the memory: the memory still gets one operation per clock, as the March test requires. The controller only has to remember that a fail belongs to the operation sent two clocks earlier.

questions.text: What selects whether the memory is driven by the functional logic or by MBIST?
options: The input mux in the collar, controlled by test_mode

questions.text: Why is the comparator usually placed **in the collar**?
options: Only a fail bit has to go back to the controller instead of the full read data.
The controller cannot compute expected data.
It removes the need for test_mode.

questions.text: What is the bypass in the collar for?
options: Making the logic around the memory testable by scan / ATPG
